title: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance: A Historical Review, a Meta-Analysis, and a Preliminary Feedback Intervention Theory rchgate.net/publication/232458848_The_Effects_of_Feedback_Interventions_on_Performance_A_Hist
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), March 31, 2025 — original paper: https://www.resea
summary: This page covers Kluger and DeNisi's landmark historical review and meta-analysis of over 600 feedback-intervention studies, which overturns the assumption that feedback reliably improves performance. Over a third of feedback interventions in the analysis actually decreased performance. To explain this variability, the authors propose Feedback Intervention Theory (FIT): feedback shifts a person's attention across a hierarchy of self-regulatory levels -- task learning, task motivation, and meta-task processes (including the self) -- and where attention lands determines whether feedback helps or hurts. Feedback that keeps attention on the task itself (its learning or its motivational goals) tends to help; feedback that redirects attention toward the self, such as normative comparisons or grades perceived as threats to self-esteem, tends to hurt or at least fails to help. Barton draws out the practical implication that feedback wording matters enormously: specific, task-focused comments increase task involvement and performance, while grades or comparative feedback that increase ego involvement do not reliably do so, and can backfire.
points: Feedback interventions do not uniformly help: in this meta-analysis of over 600 studies, more than a third of feedback interventions actually decreased performance.
Feedback Intervention Theory explains this variability by where feedback directs attention -- toward the task (helpful) or toward the self (often unhelpful or harmful).
Normative feedback that compares a student to others tends to divert attention to self-evaluation, potentially hindering performance.
Specific, task-focused comments increase task involvement and improve performance more reliably than grades or feedback that increases ego involvement.
quotes: FIs do not consistently improve student performance; they have variable effects, sometimes even decreasing performance. The meta-analysis showed that over one-third of FIs decreased performance. This suggests that the assumption that feedback always helps is incorrect
Feedback is most effective when it directs attention to the task itself (either to learning the task or increasing motivation for the task)
Feedback is less effective and can even be detrimental when it shifts attention to meta-task processes, particularly those related to the self
Normative feedback (comparing a student's performance to others) is likely to divert attention away from the task to self-evaluation, potentially hindering performance
Specific, task-focused comments are more likely to increase task involvement and improve performance compared to grades that increase ego involvement without necessarily affecting performance
